title: Spell a Target Down Increasing Columns
statement:
You have a stack of letter strips, words, all of the same length L. Think of them as rows of a table with L columns. You want to spell target one letter at a time, left to right.

To spell target[i], pick any column c and any strip whose letter in column c equals target[i]. The rule: the column you use for each letter must be strictly to the right of the column used for the previous letter. Different letters may come from different strips.

Two spellings differ if some letter uses a different column or a different strip. Return the number of spellings modulo 1 000 000 007.

examples.why: "a" in column 0 has 2 choices of strip, then "b" in column 1 or 2 has 1 each: 4. "a" in column 1 (first strip) then "b" in column 2 (first strip): 1 more.
"z" sits in column 2 and "x" in column 0. Columns must move right, so the order of letters matters.
Three letters need three different columns, and there are only two.

constraints: 1 ≤ words[i].length ≤ 1000, all strips the same length
hints: The choice of strip and the choice of column are separate. For a fixed column, does it matter which strip a letter comes from, or only how many strips have it there?
Precompute count[c][ch]: how many strips have letter ch in column c. Then a spelling is a sequence of increasing columns, weighted by the product of counts.

Let ways[i] be the number of ways to spell the first i letters using the columns seen so far. Process columns left to right; for each column, ways[i] += ways[i − 1] · count[c][target[i − 1]], with i going downward so a column is used at most once.

explain.intuition:
Strips only matter through counts. If column c has the letter "a" in 3 strips, then using column c for an "a" gives 3 choices, whichever strips they are. So first squash the table into count[c][letter]. Now the problem is: choose increasing columns c₀ < c₁ < … for the letters of target, and each choice is worth the product of its counts.

That is a classic two-index DP, like counting how many times one string appears as a subsequence of another. Let dp[c][i] be the number of ways to spell the first i letters using only columns before c. For column c you either skip it (dp[c][i]) or use it for letter i (dp[c][i] · count[c][target[i]]). Keeping only one row and updating i from high to low means each column is used for at most one letter.
steps: Build count[c][ch] for every column c and letter ch.
Let ways be an array of length m + 1 (m = target length), with ways[0] = 1.
For each column c from left to right, for i from min(m, c + 1) down to 1: add ways[i − 1] · count[c][target[i − 1]] to ways[i], modulo 10⁹ + 7.
pitfalls: Updating i from low to high. Then one column could spell two consecutive letters, like counting "aa" from a single column.
Looping over every strip inside the DP instead of using counts. That multiplies the work by the number of strips and is too slow at the limits.
Forgetting the modulo after the multiplication. The counts grow huge quickly, as in the last hand test.

solutions.title: Plain recursion over columns
solutions.idea: For each next letter, try every later column and multiply by the number of strips with that letter there. No memoization.

solutions.title: Column letter counts + DP
solutions.idea: Squash the strips into per-column letter counts, then sweep the columns once while updating the number of ways to spell each prefix of the target.

followups: Each strip may be used at most once in a spelling. Why does the count trick stop working?
Only the number of letters in target matters, not which ones: count increasing column choices. Is there a closed form?
lcTitle: Number of Ways to Form a Target String Given a Dictionary
